analysis.one_liner: Bans mortgage brokers from collecting kickbacks for steering borrowers into costlier loans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee with zero cosponsors when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Some mortgage brokers were paid a bonus, called a yield spread premium, by lenders when they talked a borrower into a loan with a higher interest rate or worse terms than the borrower actually qualified for. This bill would make it illegal for anyone who arranges a home mortgage to be paid extra money based on the terms of the loan, and would bar them from steering borrowers into loans that are not in the borrower's best interest. It was introduced in October 2007, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers and homeowners taking out mortgages. If a broker cannot earn a bigger payout by putting you in a higher-rate loan, the financial incentive to steer you into a worse deal disappears, and you are more likely to get the best terms you actually qualify for.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Truth in Lending Act to prohibit any mortgage originator from receiving, and any person from paying, incentive compensation — including yield spread premium — that is based on or varies with the terms of a residential mortgage loan [S3].

It also requires regulations that prohibit originators from steering, counseling, or directing a consumer into any mortgage that is not in the consumer's best interest, and requires rules that promote the consumer's interest in getting the best loan terms for which they qualify [S3].

The ban covers anyone who takes an application, assists a consumer in obtaining a loan, or negotiates loan terms for compensation, including people who advertise themselves as able to do so — closing the main channel through which steering incentives reached brokers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage brokers and originators whose pay was built on yield spread premiums and other loan-term-based bonuses, and the lenders that paid those bonuses to get loans placed. Consumers could also see those hidden payments disappear from the rate they were quoted.

drawbacks.text: The ban is written broadly: it prohibits any incentive compensation that varies with the terms of a loan, not just yield spread premiums, which could sweep in compensation arrangements that a supporter would have to argue were harmless or even useful [S3].

The bill leaves exceptions to regulators: the Federal Reserve Board and the Treasury Secretary may write rules creating exceptions to the prohibition, so the final shape of the ban would depend on how it was implemented [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the cost to mortgage brokers, whose business model relied on lender-paid premiums; brokers often argued such payments let borrowers fold closing costs into the loan rate, an argument the bill rejects in favor of flat compensation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to anyone taking out a home mortgage: removing the bonus a broker earns for selling you a pricier loan directly targets the steering that inflated borrowing costs for millions of households. The cost falls on brokers and lenders who relied on the payment stream, and the main design risk is that the ban is broad and its exceptions were left undefined. On balance, the consumer benefit outweighs the industry cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee in October 2007, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Murphy of Connecticut introduced the Mortgage Kickback Prevention Act on October 10, 2007 [S1][S5].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services, which was the only action it ever received [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor; the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage brokers and lenders that paid yield spread premiums kept their steering-based pay; borrowers who were being steered into costlier loans got no relief from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the sole effort behind it; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair never scheduled action)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 10, 2007 and never held a hearing or markup, letting the bill die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There is no roll-call record to judge partisan alignment: the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never came to a vote.

industries.note: Their compensation depended heavily on yield spread premiums — lender-paid bonuses that grew when a borrower accepted a worse loan. The bill removes that payment stream, which existed because borrowers paid more without knowing it [S3].

Lenders would be barred from paying loan-term-based bonuses used to induce brokers to deliver higher-rate loans. Some lenders gained volume through that practice; the bill forces them to compete on loan terms instead [S3].
